main.title: GoldenEye 007
main.summary: GoldenEye 007 is a 1997 first-person shooter game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.

cards.heading: Bond reaches Nintendo 64
cards.text: GoldenEye 007 is a 1997 first-person shooter game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is based on the 1995 James Bond film GoldenEye, with the player controlling the secret agent James Bond to prevent a criminal syndicate from using a satellite weapon. They navigate a series of levels to complete objectives, such as recovering or destroying objects, while shooting enemies. In a multiplayer mode, up to four players compete in several deathmatch scenarios via split-screen.

cards.heading: A film becomes an interactive mission
cards.text: Development began in January 1995. An inexperienced team led by Martin Hollis developed GoldenEye 007 over two and a half years. The game was conceived as a side-scrolling platform game for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, but evolved into a 3D shooter for the Nintendo 64 inspired by Doom (1993) and Virtua Cop (1994). Rare visited the GoldenEye set for reference, and Eon Productions and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM) allowed them to expand the game with sequences and characters not featured in the film.

cards.heading: Release and reception
cards.text: GoldenEye 007 was released in Japan on 23 August 1997, North America on 25 August 1997, and the United Kingdom on 7 November 1997, two years after the release of the film but shortly before the release of its sequel Tomorrow Never Dies. It faced low expectations from the gaming media during development. However, it received critical acclaim and sold over eight million copies, making it the third-best-selling Nintendo 64 game. The game was praised for its visuals, gameplay depth and variety, and multiplayer mode. In 1998, it received the BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Award, as well as four awards from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.

cards.heading: The console shooter and its legacy
cards.text: GoldenEye 007 demonstrated the viability of home consoles as platforms for first-person shooters and signalled a transition from Doom-like shooters to a more grounded style. It pioneered features such as atmospheric single-player missions, widescreen gaming, stealth elements, and console multiplayer deathmatch. The game is considered to be one of the most influential and greatest video games ever made, with many of its elements, such as the Klobb gun, leaving an enduring impression in video game culture. A spiritual successor, Perfect Dark, was released in 2000, while a remake developed by Eurocom, also titled GoldenEye 007, was released in 2010. The original game was rereleased in January 2023 on Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S via Xbox Game Pass and Nintendo Switch via the Nintendo Classics service.

cards.heading: Two days after the Japanese launch
cards.text: GoldenEye 007 reached North America on August 25, 1997, two days after its Japanese release. Rare's adaptation organised Bond's work around mission objectives, alarms, rooms and routes. It also offered four-player split-screen matches, a mode added late in development. These different ways to play helped make the film licence a distinctive console shooter.

cards.heading: Learning each mission’s objectives
cards.text: A mission can require photographing a target, retrieving a key, sabotaging equipment or protecting a character. Higher difficulty settings add objectives, encouraging players to learn more of each level. Guards, cameras and alarms can reward a cautious approach before gunfire begins. Completing Bond's assignment involves understanding what must be done in a space as well as surviving its enemies.

cards.heading: Four players share a screen
cards.text: Four-player multiplayer divides one television into separate views of the match. Players compete through different scenarios, weapons and maps while sitting beside one another. The arrangement also allows them to see an opponent's screen, making screen-peeking part of the shared experience. What began late in development became one of the game's most familiar features.

cards.heading: Adapting the film into missions
cards.text: Rare used the film's locations and characters to create missions with room for exploration and repeated attempts. During development, the team visited the GoldenEye set for reference. Eon Productions and MGM also allowed sequences and characters beyond those shown in the film. That freedom let the designers build objectives and routes around the actions the player would perform as Bond.

main.title: Total Annihilation
main.summary: Total Annihilation is a science fiction real-time strategy video game released in September 1997 for Microsoft Windows and Mac OS by Cavedog Entertainment and distributed internationally by GT Interactive.

cards.heading: Cavedog’s science-fiction strategy game
cards.text: Total Annihilation is a science fiction real-time strategy video game released in September 1997 for Microsoft Windows and Mac OS by Cavedog Entertainment and distributed internationally by GT Interactive. Two expansion packs were released in 1998, The Core Contingency on April 29 and Battle Tactics on July 20, while a medieval-themed spin-off called Total Annihilation: Kingdoms was released on June 25, 1999.

cards.heading: The rights pass to new owners
cards.text: Rights to the game passed to Infogrames (later Atari) following the 1999 acquisition and closure of Cavedog Entertainment's parent company, Humongous Entertainment. In July 2013, Wargaming bought the Total Annihilation franchise from Atari's bankruptcy proceedings.

cards.heading: Mods, Spring and Supreme Commander
cards.text: Total Annihilation has been re-released on Steam and GOG, but is no longer actively supported. The creators of XTA, a mod for Total Annihilation, independently developed the open-source 3D graphics Spring game engine. The Total Annihilation 3D project began in 2006. Former lead designer Chris Taylor went on to found Gas Powered Games which created Supreme Commander in 2007, considered the "spiritual successor" of Total Annihilation.

main.title: Fallout
main.subtitle: Leaving the Vault to find a water chip
main.summary: Interplay’s 1997 RPG sends a Vault dweller into a post-nuclear world where skills, dialogue and combat open different ways forward.

cards.heading: Interplay’s post-nuclear role-playing game
cards.text: Interplay's Fallout sends a Vault dweller into a post-nuclear world to find a replacement water chip. Its S.P.E.C.I.A.L. attributes, skills, dialogue and combat let characters approach situations in different ways. Communities and competing interests fill a wasteland shaped by atomic retrofuturism. Steam lists September 30, 1997, as the product date, while Bethesda generally places the series' debut in October 1997.

cards.heading: A deadline for the Vault
cards.text: A failing water chip threatens the protagonist's home. Finding a replacement gives the journey an urgent objective as the player learns what lies beyond the Vault. A settlement can supply help, information or a delay, and the search unfolds under a deadline. The sheltered community that raised the character depends on discoveries made in an unfamiliar outside world.

cards.heading: Choosing strengths and limitations
cards.text: Character creation assigns strengths and limitations through S.P.E.C.I.A.L. attributes and skills. The player cannot maximise every ability, so choices affect which approaches are practical. A technical problem may reward one skill while a conversation calls on another. Building a different character can reveal another solution to a familiar situation, giving later playthroughs a different course.

cards.heading: Negotiating another way forward
cards.text: Conversations can uncover information, allow negotiation and sometimes avoid a fight. Available responses depend on the character's abilities and circumstances, making social skills useful alongside weapons and technical knowledge. The player must consider what an interlocutor wants and which answers the character can support. Persuasion can change how a conflict develops before combat begins.

main.title: Age of Empires
main.summary: Age of Empires is a 1997 real-time strategy video game based on the ancient world, developed by Ensemble Studios and published by Microsoft, and the first game in the Age of Empires series.

cards.heading: Four ages of the ancient world
cards.text: Age of Empires is a 1997 real-time strategy video game based on the ancient world, developed by Ensemble Studios and published by Microsoft, and the first game in the Age of Empires series. The game uses the Genie Engine, a 2D sprite-based game engine. The game allows the user to act as the leader of an ancient civilization by advancing it through four ages (the Stone, Tool, Bronze, and Iron Ages), gaining access to new and improved units with each advance.

cards.heading: The Rise of Rome and later editions
cards.text: The game received positive reviews, and an expansion pack, titled The Rise of Rome, was released in 1998. The game is now generally regarded as one of the best video games ever made. Both the original Age of Empires and the expansion pack were later released as "The Gold Edition". The first sequel, Age of Empires II, was released in 1999. Age of Empires: Definitive Edition, a remastered version of the game, was released on February 20, 2018.

main.title: Riven
main.summary: Riven: The Sequel to Myst is a 1997 adventure game developed by Cyan Productions and published by Red Orb Entertainment for Mac OS and Microsoft Windows.

cards.heading: Atrus sends the player to Riven
cards.text: Riven: The Sequel to Myst is a 1997 adventure game developed by Cyan Productions and published by Red Orb Entertainment for Mac OS and Microsoft Windows. It is the sequel to 1993's Myst, and the second installment of the Myst series. The game's story is set after the events of its predecessor; having rescued Atrus, who had been trapped by his sons, the player character is enlisted by him to free his wife from his power-hungry father, Gehn. Riven takes place almost entirely on the Age of Riven, a world slowly falling apart due to Gehn's destructive rule.

cards.heading: Designing a world beyond Myst
cards.text: Development of Riven began soon after Myst became a success, and spanned more than three years. In an effort to create a visual style distinct from that of Myst, director Robyn Miller and his brother, producer Rand Miller, recruited production designer Richard Vander Wende as a co-director. Broderbund employed a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign to publicize the game's release. Riven received ports to the PlayStation, Sega Saturn, Pocket PC, iOS and Android.

cards.heading: Reception and a later reimagining
cards.text: Riven was praised by reviewers, with the magazine Salon proclaiming that the game approaches the level of art. Critics positively noted the puzzles and immersive experience of the gameplay, though publications such as Edge felt that the nature of point-and-click gameplay limited the title heavily. The best-selling game of 1997, Riven sold 1.5 million copies in one year. After the game's release, Robyn Miller left Cyan to form his own development studio, ending the professional partnership of the two brothers. Rand stayed at Cyan and continued to work on Myst-related products including The Myst Reader and the real-time rendered game Uru: Ages Beyond Myst. The next entry in the Myst series, Myst III: Exile, was developed by Presto Studios and published by Ubisoft. A remake of the game, recreating the world in fully explorable 3D and supporting virtual reality, was released in June 2024.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: Colony Wars
main.subtitle: A pilot inside a larger war
main.summary: Colony Wars is Psygnosis's 1997 PlayStation space-combat game, first released in North America on 4 November. The League of Free Worlds fights an Earth empire that draws resources from its colonies. The player enters that struggle as a pilot, flying the craft assigned to each mission rather than controlling the whole war. Battles range across space with fighters, larger vessels and specific objectives. Success matters, but the campaign also accommodates failure, allowing the story to continue along a different route instead of always demanding that an unsuccessful mission be repeated.

cards.heading: A pilot inside a larger war
cards.text: Colony Wars is Psygnosis's 1997 PlayStation space-combat game, first released in North America on 4 November. The League of Free Worlds fights an Earth empire that draws resources from its colonies. The player enters that struggle as a pilot, flying the craft assigned to each mission rather than controlling the whole war. Battles range across space with fighters, larger vessels and specific objectives. Success matters, but the campaign also accommodates failure, allowing the story to continue along a different route instead of always demanding that an unsuccessful mission be repeated.

cards.heading: The ship for the assignment
cards.text: High Command selects the starfighter, giving each mission a particular combination of weapons and capabilities. Energy weapons, missiles and torpedoes answer different targets; some craft also carry nonlethal EMP cannons. Countermeasures help escape incoming missiles, while a grapple gun can secure important objects. The player must read the assigned equipment alongside the objective. A mission is therefore more than clearing everything from the view: the available weapons help define what should be destroyed, disabled or recovered, and which threats have to be survived while that work is completed.

cards.heading: Failure opens another route
cards.text: Missions are grouped into acts, with performance directing the campaign through branching paths. Certain encounters become turning points, so a lost engagement need not end the war or produce the same outcome as another defeat. Combat records let the player review the service already completed. A voiced database describes ships and planets, supplying context beyond the immediate cockpit view. Tim Wright composed the score. Colony Wars: Vengeance followed in 1998 and Red Sun in 2000, extending a series that gave PlayStation players both space battles and a campaign shaped by their results.

main.title: Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back
main.summary: Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back is a 1997 platform game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.

cards.text: Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back is a 1997 platform game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. It is a sequel to Crash Bandicoot (1996), and is part of the Crash Bandicoot series. Taking place on a fictional group of islands near Australia, Crash Bandicoot 2 follows the adventures of the anthropomorphic bandicoot named Crash. Crash is abducted by series villain Doctor Neo Cortex, who tricks him into thinking he wants to save the world. Crash is thrust into several parts of N. Sanity Island in order to gather crystals that will allow Cortex to contain the power of an upcoming planetary alignment and keep the planet from being destroyed. Crash's sister Coco and Cortex's former assistant Doctor Nitrus Brio try to warn him about Cortex, with the latter urging Crash to gather gems instead of crystals.

Cortex Strikes Back received positive reviews from critics and is widely considered to be superior to its predecessor. Much of the praise went to the game's graphics, controls and music, while criticisms focused on the trial-and-error gameplay, lack of level variety, easy boss levels and lack of innovation as a platform game. The game went on to become one of the best-selling PlayStation video games of all time and replaced its predecessor as the highest-selling Western title in Japan at the time, selling more than 800,000 copies in the country by April 1998. A remake was released as a part of the Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy in 2017.

main.title: Einhänder
main.subtitle: One arm for the next weapon
main.summary: Einhänder is Square's PlayStation scrolling shooter, released in Japan on 20 November 1997. A pilot from the Moon enters enemy territory on Earth during a future war, gathering information and weapons. The spacecraft's single manipulator arm supplies the game's name and central action: enemy gunpods can be taken and attached to the fighter. Three-dimensional scenery changes the camera's view, while movement remains on a two-dimensional plane. The result gives a familiar side-scrolling advance a changing sense of scale as buildings, machinery and hostile craft pass around the player.

cards.heading: One arm for the next weapon
cards.text: Einhänder is Square's PlayStation scrolling shooter, released in Japan on 20 November 1997. A pilot from the Moon enters enemy territory on Earth during a future war, gathering information and weapons. The spacecraft's single manipulator arm supplies the game's name and central action: enemy gunpods can be taken and attached to the fighter. Three-dimensional scenery changes the camera's view, while movement remains on a two-dimensional plane. The result gives a familiar side-scrolling advance a changing sense of scale as buildings, machinery and hostile craft pass around the player.

cards.heading: Choosing where a gun belongs
cards.text: A standard machine gun remains available, but captured gunpods provide weapons with different reach, ammunition and power. A cannon, guided missiles or a large energy blade changes the useful distance from a target. The arm can hold a pod above or below the craft, altering its firing angle or direction. Ammunition runs out, so a powerful attachment is also a temporary opportunity. Choosing when to use it and where to carry it ties the next attack to what enemies have already left behind, rather than to a fixed selection made before the stage.

cards.heading: Keeping the chain moving
cards.text: Destroying enemy cores builds a hit counter and increases the points awarded for further cores. Hesitation lets that counter fall; reaching a high multiplier creates a short period of larger bonuses. Bosses often have separate parts around a main core, giving the player several things to read and dismantle during one confrontation. Kenichiro Fukui's techno- and trance-oriented score supports the mechanical setting. Critics praised the graphics and shooting, while noting the short duration and lack of two-player play. The North American release followed in May 1998, with the original game later returning on Japan's PlayStation Network.

main.title: Tomb Raider II
main.summary: Tomb Raider II (also known as Tomb Raider II: Starring Lara Croft) is a 1997 action-adventure video game developed by Core Design and published by Eidos Interactive.

cards.heading: Lara searches for the Dagger of Xian
cards.text: Tomb Raider II (also known as Tomb Raider II: Starring Lara Croft) is a 1997 action-adventure video game developed by Core Design and published by Eidos Interactive. It was first released on Windows and PlayStation. Later releases came for Mac OS (1998), iOS (2014) and Android (2015). It is the second entry in the Tomb Raider series, and follows archaeologist-adventurer Lara Croft hunting the magical Dagger of Xian in competition with an Italian cult. Gameplay features Lara navigating levels split into multiple areas and room complexes while fighting enemies and solving puzzles to progress, with some areas allowing for or requiring the use of vehicles.

cards.heading: Six to nine months under pressure
cards.text: Production began in 1996 immediately after the success of the original Tomb Raider, being completed in between six and nine months, a short development period which was physically and emotionally stressful for the team. Original staff members Toby Gard and Paul Douglas left over creative differences with Eidos, though many remained including composer Nathan McCree. A Sega Saturn version was scrapped due to technical limitations and a console exclusivity deal signed between Eidos and Sony.

cards.heading: The Golden Mask and a later remaster
cards.text: Tomb Raider II was well-received by critics upon its release, with many noting its expanded gameplay and smoother graphics. It went on to sell nearly seven million copies worldwide. An expansion pack entitled The Further Adventures of Lara Croft was in development in late 1997 but was cancelled. Some elements from the project were carried over to the 1998 sequel, Tomb Raider III. An expansion entitled The Golden Mask was released the following year, containing new levels focused on Lara's quest to find a golden mask in Alaska. A remastered version of the game, alongside The Golden Mask, was included in Tomb Raider I–III Remastered in 2024.
